summary: Looks at an ambiguity in how the retransmission-allowed element of PIDF-LO location data should be interpreted when carried in SIP. It gives recommendations for how SIP location conveyance should handle it. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A note says whether someone may pass your location on. People read the note differently, so this explains how to read it when it travels in phone-call messages.

questions: location by reference vs by value
subtitle: How to read the PIDF-LO retransmission-allowed flag when location rides inside SIP requests, and what to do about it.

tldr.problem: The retransmission-allowed element of a location object was designed for a model with a Location Server, but in SIP the location may pass through many intermediaries, so it is unclear who counts as an authorized recipient.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC recommends that SIP entities handling a message be treated as authorized recipients, that access be limited by not sending location, by sending it by reference, or by encrypting it, and that a new Location-Routing-Allowed header say whether location may be used for routing.
tldr.outcome: It records the GEOPRIV working group consensus for the SIP working group. The header is an exemplary proposal, and the actual SIP syntax is left to the SIP working group.

today: RFC 5606 is an Informational document from August 2009, and the metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. It states consensus guidance for the SIP working group and leaves the actual SIP syntax to that group.

sections.title: Location Objects Inside SIP
sections.content:
The Presence Information Data Format for Location Objects (PIDF-LO, RFC 4119) carries location information (LI) along with policy set by the Rule Maker, as described in RFC 3693. The policy can limit how long recipients keep LI and whether they may pass it on.

The Session Initiation Protocol (SIP, RFC 3261) is one using protocol for PIDF-LO. The common reason to put location in SIP is to let it influence routing. The RFC gives emergency services and a taxi call as examples.
sections.eli5: Some phone-call messages carry where you are, plus your rules about who may share it. That raises questions about how the rules work.

sections.title: The Ambiguity
sections.content:
The <retransmission-allowed> element was designed for the RFC 3693 model, where location flows from a Location Generator through a Location Server to a Location Recipient. The server enforces access rules, and the element is meant to stop an authorized recipient from sharing location with third parties. The RFC's example is a pizza shop selling a customer's location to an advertiser. It is only an expression of the Rule Maker's preferences, not a protocol-level protection against eavesdropping.

SIP differs. A request may cross several intermediaries before reaching the user agent server, and some may inspect the location to do location-based routing. There is no Location Server picking recipients, and the sender cannot easily predict which intermediaries or final target will see it. Location can also be sent by reference (a URL) instead of by value.

The question is hardest when the element is set to no, which is the default. Must a proxy that routes on location strip it or refuse to forward? Must every proxy that understands RFC 4119 parse the policy? The RFC lists these questions without answering all of them there.
sections.eli5: The rule says do not share my location. But a phone call is passed along by many helpers. Which helpers count as allowed to see it, and which count as outsiders?

sections.title: Core Semantics and Goals
sections.content:
After extensive discussion in the GEOPRIV and SIP contexts, the stated goal is that location-based routing must work even when <retransmission-allowed> is no. A solution should also let the Rule Maker allow or forbid using location for routing, and for consumption by the endpoint.

The consensus is that any SIP entity that receives a message containing location through normal SIP routing, or as a result of location-based routing, is an authorized recipient. One SIP element may therefore pass location to another even if <retransmission-allowed> is no, because that counts as delivery to authorized recipients and not retransmission. Passing messages outside normal routing to external parties is still not allowed, since that is what the element is meant to control.
sections.eli5: Helpers that pass the call along the normal route may see the location and hand it to the next helper. Sending it to strangers off to the side is still not allowed.

sections.title: Ways to Limit Access
sections.content:
Three mechanisms are described.

  • Public key encryption. The originator encrypts the PIDF-LO for a known entity, even in several versions. It needs a public key for that entity and a key discovery system, so the working group does not consider it an appropriate baseline.
  • Location by reference. The SIP request carries a URL and location is conveyed only when it is dereferenced. Then the meaning of <retransmission-allowed> is clear: each entity that receives location during dereferencing is bound by it. The Rule Maker can influence who gets what detail, using whitelists or blacklists. Authentication costs vary, for example SIP Digest is cheap but needs pre-established keys, while RFC 4474 Identity needs no pre-association but is heavier.
  • Not including location. The most basic option. If location turns out to be required, an error can be returned and communication continued with it included, at the price of slower setup.

Recommended choice: omit location if it should be revealed to no one on the path. Location by reference is generally the most deployable way to limit access. Encryption may suit limited cases where location by value must be used.
sections.eli5: You can lock the location in a box only one helper can open, give helpers a ticket to ask you for it, or just not send it unless someone really needs it. The ticket idea works best.

sections.title: The Location-Routing-Allowed Header
sections.content:
To limit the use made of location, the RFC proposes, as an exemplary concrete idea, a SIP Location-Routing-Allowed header. Yes means the Rule Maker permits using the included location for location-based routing, and No means it does not. Like <retransmission-allowed>, it has no enforcement mechanism. If a reference comes with No, elements need not try to dereference it, which is faster than being refused at authentication.

The recommendations are:

  • It should be mandatory to implement for elements complying with the location conveyance document.
  • It should appear in any SIP message that contains a location, by reference or by value.
  • A message with location but no such header is treated as if it were set to no.
  • A user agent may insert it even without including a location, to set policy for locations that the network adds later.
  • An element inserting a location adds the header if none is present, and does not override an existing one.
  • An element that is neither the originator nor inserting a location should not insert it.

For back-to-back user agents acting as simple intermediaries, <retransmission-allowed> does not apply, and they must copy the location and the policy values. When one acts as an endpoint, ending one session and starting another, it must not copy the location if <retransmission-allowed> is no.
sections.eli5: A small label on the call says whether helpers may use your location to pick where the call goes. No label means no. Nothing physically stops a rude helper, but polite ones follow it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The security considerations section says only that the privacy and security implications of distributing location information are the fundamental subject of the document. The mechanisms above are advisory. Neither <retransmission-allowed> nor the proposed header is enforced by the protocol, and encryption and location by reference are the tools that actually restrict who sees location.
sections.eli5: The whole document is about keeping location private. The labels are polite requests, while locking it up or handing out tickets really limits who sees it.
